segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Why aren't you more mad?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: I think I'm just too tired to be mad. It's like, when I think of it, I get exhausted. I get a little desperate. I feel like a little bit like-- I feel a little bit, like, underwater.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is my coworker, Sean Cole, who's a producer here on the radio show. And the thing that brought him to this state is a bed-- a bed he does not have. He ordered it back in September when he moved to a new apartment.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And this is where I've been sleeping since I moved in-- on the floor, on my old mattress, awaiting my new bed.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Just to be clear, the mattress for the new bed arrived right away after he ordered it. It's rolled up like a burrito near the window. The issue is the bed frame and the headboard. They're still AWOL, undelivered, absent, four months after ordering. And I'm talking to Sean about this because today's program is about all kinds of different sorts of runarounds, and he is in the middle of a sort of classic one, one lots of us have experienced.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For the record, the bed that he ordered is a queen-sized bed from the Casper online store. As a podcast producer, he told me he felt like a living cliche ordering a product that is advertised on so many podcasts, but he says he really liked the bed. It's got an angled, cushioned headboard to lean against when you're reading at night. Sean is somebody who's never really fixed up a place with nice furniture, and he was finally getting around to it, and he was excited. And at first, the delay was a completely excusable kind of thing. The bed was backordered, which, you know, happens with furniture.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It was supposed to be ready for delivery on November 18. But the 18th of November comes, 18th of November goes, it does not show up. Sean reaches out to Casper.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: They said, you'll hear from our delivery partner. OK, get a text from the delivery partner. It was a company I had never heard of, called RXO. RXO texts me and says, hi, we have scheduled your delivery for September 26. And I'm like, it hasn't been September 26 for, like, two months.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sean calls RXO and reschedules the delivery, this time for a date that's in the future, not the past. But this is the first of what will be many texts and communications from RXO that make no sense at all.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The new delivery date is in three weeks. That day finally arrives.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: I get up, strip the mattress, pull it off of the floor, set it up so it'll make it easier for them to take away.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So it's leaning against which wall?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: It was leaning against the wall in the office, against my books. I wait for them to come.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Around 10:00, he gets a text telling him his bed will not be delivered. He needs to reschedule. He calls to find out why.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And they said, oh, yeah. No, we can't bring it to you because you asked for the haul away service to take away your old mattress.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But couldn't this truck still drop off your thing, even if they weren't going to haul away the old mattress?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Right. Yeah. Good question. Like, why does not being able to take something away prevent you from bringing me something?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The delivery is rescheduled for Monday, a few days later. Monday comes. They text, saying it's going to be Tuesday. No explanation why. An hour and a half after that, they text again, saying that now it won't be delivered Tuesday.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And so I call them, and I'm like, what's the deal? And they go, oh, there's been a truck breakdown. And I was like, oh. So when can it come now? And they go, oh, hang on a second. And they look at their notes or whatever. And they go, oh, no, no, wait. You are good for tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And I was like, I am good for tomorrow? They were like, yeah, because it's already been added to the route. And I'm like, isn't there a truck breakdown? Like, what-- you know, like, was that just something you said? Like-- and I still don't know the answer to that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I have to say, this is one of the most annoying things about this kind of runaround. At every stage, you get answers that leave you sort of squinting and scratching your head, trying to understand them. Every explanation is a non-explanation.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So then, Tuesday, I get up again. I strip the bed. I pick the mattress up off the floor. I lean it up against the wall. And then I get a text saying, your delivery is confirmed for Thursday.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This time when he calls, there's no explanation at all, just an apology. Thursday comes.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And on Thursday, I get up. I do not strip the bed, nor do I pull the mattress off the floor, because beginning to learn.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of course, it doesn't come.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: And I call them, and I'm like, what's going on? Then they go, oh, there's a hard hold on this order. And I'm like, why is there a hard hold? And they go, oh, there was a duplicate on the order docket, two bed frames and headboards here that are scheduled for shipment for the same person.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They thought it might be a mistake, and they didn't want to ship until they knew. Sean wonders why didn't they just contact him and ask if he ordered two beds. And also, has this been on his paperwork from the start?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Then that's always been the case, right? Like, why am I only finding out about this now? And that means, like, it was never going to come or something? And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And now you're wondering, is this even true that there's a problem in the paperwork?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Well, no, because it seemed so specific. Like, why would you make up something like that? Unless it's just like-- I don't know. I don't know. I guess the answer is, I don't know, and it's maddening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then, after thinking they had to deliver two beds to Sean, they admitted they didn't have any. They did a week-long dock search, finally showed up with a bed, but it was the wrong size, which put Sean back at square one. Early on, Sean started to keep a record of all these interactions with RXO and Casper. And at this point, it is 18 pages long.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: If this document were a poem, what would it be called?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: (LAUGHING) It would be called--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sean's a published poet, by the way.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: --uh, "How Do You Sleep?"

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When we reached out to RXO and Casper, the bed company, to find out how they do sleep at night, given their treatment of Sean Cole, the answer was refreshingly honest. Casper's VP of operations emailed admitting, yeah, the last few years, because global supply chains have been so crazy, Casper has experienced, quote, "a myriad of disruptions."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He did say that only a tiny portion of the shipping is done with RXO, and they're trying to work with RXO to improve things. 90% of their customers, he said, rate their experience with RXO favorably, meaning 10% do not. Sean is 1 in 10. Pretty bad odds, if you ask me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: My take is that they never actually had a bed for him. Sean feels like he's come this far, he doesn't want to start over with a different company. A runaround hits different people different ways.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: I'm the perfect person to give the runaround to because I am preternaturally indisposed to flipping out-- you know, demanding a result.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You're saying you wouldn't do these things.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: I would not do these things. I'm the person who you want to give the runaround to because, like, I'm not going to, like, reach through the phone and try to strangle you. Like, even when I freak out, I'm polite about it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: True. Sean can get a little worked up talking to me about all this, but the harshest he ever got with Casper or RXO is a sternly-worded email that sounds like it was written by an English gentleman in the year 1820. Quote, "This is beyond unacceptable. Please let me know what Casper intends to do to rectify this situation. Yours, sincerely."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A runaround-- where you float in that weird information limbo where you can't tell what the truth is, where you don't get what you want, in a contest of wills with some other person or entity, and it goes on, and on, and on, it just doesn't end, it tests you. It shows you who you are.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, some very different kinds of runarounds and some very different reactions to them from people who are being pushed to their very limits. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, "Like the Show 48 Hours, Except a Lot More Hours." So this first story is about somebody who, like Sean, is being given the runaround, but the runaround is about something much more consequential to her life than a bed frame. And the woman it's happening to, over and over, she has to decide whether to cut her losses and walk away, or stay with it and fight her way through. Reporter Brenna Smith, who first wrote about this for the news site, the Baltimore Banner, explains.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Even before this whole thing began, Renee's life involved a lot of running around. She's busy-- got three kids, works days and nights as a home health aide. When money's tight, she also drives for DoorDash and Instacart.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: She spends a lot of time in her car, like a lot of busy people. But unlike a lot of busy people, Renee told me and my producer Chris, she usually chooses the slowest possible route to her next destination because--

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I'm scared of beltways. I mean, I don't do beltways. I take the long way everywhere.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: What do you mean you're scared of beltways?

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I'm just scared of all the traffic-- like, so many different lanes with cars. I have real bad anxiety. My nerves are bad. So I think it's just, like, so many different lanes with just so many cars flying past you, so I just prefer not to. I'd rather go on side roads.

segments.speaker: Chris
segments.text: Is there, like, a Renee speed limit? Like, above this--

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Yeah, I don't like to go any past like 45.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Renee's commitment to the local roads just outside of Baltimore, where she lives, will sometimes add 20, 30, even 40 minutes to her trips. So that's Renee.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The story I want to tell you started last spring when something went wrong with Renee's SNAP benefits-- her food stamps. Her monthly money stopped appearing on her benefits card. Fixing this took five or six trips to the social services office, filling out tons of paperwork, and three months of waiting. This isn't unusual for her or anyone on benefits.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Finally, a kind woman at the front desk at social services looked into her case and found some glitch in the system. She fixed it for Renee, and the next morning, everything was made right. All three months of missed benefits showed up at once. She now had almost $3,000 on her card, the highest she'd ever had. Renee felt a wave of relief. But a couple of weeks later, Renee went online to check the balance on her card.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: And everything was gone, except $66. That's all I can really remember. I thought it was a mistake. I thought, well, let me get off the app. And I cleared it out and tried it again, same thing.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: She called the number on the back of the card to make sure and found out, again, $66. First, she was just confused. And then she noticed large transactions at stores she's never visited near Washington, D.C., where she never goes, because beltways. She realized someone had somehow stolen her SNAP money. The thousands of dollars she'd just gotten back on her card was gone in one afternoon. And this is where her runaround began.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: I've been reporting on social services, like SNAP in Maryland, and I've seen SNAP fraud happening a lot. Benefits theft skyrocketed from $90,000 in 2021 to over $1.5 dollars in 2022. SNAP fraud is actually up across the US.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The night it happened to Renee, she couldn't stop crying and couldn't sleep. This is money she used to buy food for her kids. Without it, she'd have to pick up extra jobs, get behind on rent. So the next morning, she marched into the same government building she'd been in so many times before to fix the problem in person. Maybe she'd get the nice lady again.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I went down to the social services, and the same lady that fixed the food stamps was like, yeah, I remember. I just fixed them for you. And all the money that, you know, was going to come on your card-- she was almost in tears. She said, I feel so bad for you, because it's so much. She said, I've never seen that much be taken at once. She said, but I can tell you now, they're not going to-- they're not going to refund anything.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The woman told Renee, because the stolen SNAP money is actually federal money, Maryland couldn't pay her back. It was a statewide policy.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: She said, there was nothing-- she said, I really wish we could help you. And then of course, everybody in the whole-- because you know, you're sitting there with all these people. And the window, everybody can hear you talk, because you're only walking a couple of steps to the window.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: And you know, you've got the whole room looking at you at one time, so I felt so stupid. I'm crying. And I don't-- I don't like crying in front of people. I try to hold my emotions back. And it was hard that day. I just couldn't hold it back.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: I first met Renee on this Facebook group for parents in Maryland who use benefits like SNAP. There were lots of parents, mostly moms, writing in, saying they had had their benefits stolen. And there was Renee, posting all the time about what had happened to her and really trying to help everyone else. "Everyone, please read this," she wrote. "If we all come together and report this to the police and social services, then something may be done." There were lots of moms who had tried to get social services to refund them. No luck. They'd also filed reports with their local police. Nothing.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: I talked to dozens of them, and Renee was in a category of her own. She did far more than anyone else. When I got her on the phone back then, she'd been playing phone and email tag for days, bouncing between every authority figure she could find-- the Office of the Inspector General for Maryland's Social Services, the USDA in D.C., which funds SNAP, even the Maryland legislature where she called delegate after delegate, but it all got her nowhere.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I just spoke to Delegate Robin Grammar, I think his name is, yesterday. And he told me that, unfortunately, no matter what I do, he said they're not going to refund the money.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The police weren't any help either. The cop assigned to her case, Officer Timothy Valis, would sometimes take days to answer her texts, and didn't seem to be doing anything. He was a rookie who hadn't graduated the academy yet. So Renee did something I haven't seen anyone else do. She decided to investigate her own case. She was going to find the people who took her SNAP money.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: One thing about Renee, she loves true crime shows, like 48 Hours. So she knew how important the first couple of days are in any investigation. She was worried time was slipping away, so she went to the facts she had.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The SNAP benefits app had given her the details for every fraudulent transaction, all seven of them. They included a dollar amount, a date, and the name of each store. There had been big purchases, some over $500. Renee thought that maybe those stores could rewind their security footage to the times of those transactions and maybe identify the thieves. She texts all this to Officer Valis.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I said, I looked at my food stamp app on my phone and wanted to let you know I found all the store numbers that these people used my food stamp card. I sent him the picture of all that. Then he said, OK, thank you. And then I said--

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: She suggested the police contact the stores, but nothing happened. So--

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I called the stores myself.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Most of the stores wouldn't help her. They don't show surveillance footage to customers, only police. But one manager at an international market agreed to check.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: And they pulled the video of the people that did it.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: So she sent me one, two, three, four, five pictures, and one four-second video of them just driving away.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: And all of a sudden, Renee was looking at the faces of the people who stole from her, security footage from a Sunday in early August. It looked to be during the day. It was bright out. The photo was grainy, but she could make out a middle-aged man exiting the store. Then, in a different photo, a woman with a low bun and a blue-striped skirt with a shopping cart.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: And you see in the back of the cart, the people that stole it, they bought cases and cases of baby formula.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: So they didn't buy groceries. These people bought cases of baby formula. It's on the picture.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: $1,200 of baby formula, which seems weird, but it makes sense if you think about it. Formula is a very efficient way to convert food stamps into cash. It's in every grocery store. It doesn't go bad quickly, like meat. It's dense, so you can pack a lot of it into your car. And in the summer of 2022, there was a shortage of it.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Renee had found the suspects and the getaway car. The footage showed them driving off in a Toyota minivan. But she still had no idea how to find out their names, their identities. And even after squinting every which way at the photos of the license plate, she still couldn't make out what it was.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: If you look at it from a certain way, you could see a little better. But then once you really start to-- it's confusing. It's really hard to-- so I just kind of took that and sent that to the officer.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: When Renee texted all this to Officer Valis, he didn't say much. Just, quote, "I updated the report with the information you've given me." He also said he'd referred her case to the department's investigative and cybercrime units. Then he stopped responding, for weeks.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: So now he's not answering any of my texts asking if he has found anything else out, nothing.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: He has not responded to you since August 13.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Nothing. No answer. I'm just like-- I just feel like people don't really care because it's not someone close to them that has needed food stamps. And this is not like $100. I wouldn't even probably even call if it was something small. This is almost $3,000. And this is not from me, this is from my children-- it's taken from my kids.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Then, in late August, Renee receives a letter from social services. It says they looked into her case and, quote, "did not find a system error or that the card was used fraudulently." There would be no refund.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Other moms on the Facebook group had gotten the same letter, and a lot of them had given up at that point. But Renee reads the fine print. She noticed that the bottom of the letter offered her the chance to appeal this finding before a judge, with evidence.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I think it's called, like, some kind of fair hearing or something from social services. And I've got to prove that it wasn't me, even though it's clearly these people. I have to prove that and try to fight that in, you know, court or wherever.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: So she was going to file an appeal. It was a lot of money. And some part of her just wanted to prove that this thing had actually happened to her, that she had been robbed. All she had was grainy footage from one of the stores. She wanted a stronger case. If she could get better quality security footage from another store, maybe she could identify the license plate, which could lead you to the criminals.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: She wanted to go in person. But again, these stores were near Washington D.C., a beltway, an interstate highway, and another beltway away. And her car wasn't in great shape. And so--

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: OK, we're recording. Let's see. OK. We're going to be there at 10:36.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: And that's how I wound up picking up Renee at her red brick rowhouse outside Baltimore on a muggy August day to drive to D.C. We managed to find a time for this after Renee performed some serious scheduling gymnastics-- got a babysitter, moved around her hectic work schedule. I recognized her from Facebook, a white lady in her 30s with a round face and big green eyes. Renee was so competent on the phone. But today, faced with the prospect of doing in-person detective work, she's nervous again.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I don't need anything, right?

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: No, I don't think you need to take anything. I think you just need to come in and--

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Just go?

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Yeah, just explain who you are and why you're there. OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We stopped right outside D.C., a CVS. Renee had already called the store and talked to a guy named Keith, a manager. We walk in to find him.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Hi. Oh, I spoke to you. Keith. You're a manager too?

segments.speaker: CVS Employee 1
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Oh, OK. I'm the one that spoke to him about the baby formula that was stolen.

segments.speaker: CVS Employee 1
segments.text: Yeah-- oh.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: They tell Renee what everyone else did-- they're only allowed to show security footage to law enforcement. But, they add, there is a police station a couple blocks away.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: So if I went there--

segments.speaker: CVS Employee 2
segments.text: Yeah, you go in there.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: They would come right over here and--

segments.speaker: CVS Employee 2
segments.text: I don't know if they'll come right over here, but--

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: So if they come back here-- if they do, which they probably won't, but then you'll be able to show them?

segments.speaker: CVS Employee 2
segments.text: Yeah, all right.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: OK. OK.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Within minutes, we're standing outside the police department for the small town of Seat Pleasant, Maryland, telling Renee's story. She explains that she had had her food stamps stolen. One of the cops has a hard time understanding how this crime had gone down. Specifically, how the thieves got their own card.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Because the police in my area--

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: Do they copy your information?

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: They're saying--

segments.speaker: Photographer
segments.text: They skim it.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: He had my card, even though I have my card. They had a card. Like, we have--

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: They have to have your PIN number too.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Yeah. He said skimmers do that.

segments.speaker: Photographer
segments.text: Well, when you skim, they punch in the PINs.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: A skimmer is a device that thieves put over card scanners. It looks just like a card scanner, so you can't tell. It can capture your card information, including your PIN. Most EBT cards-- the benefits cards people on assistance, like Renee, use to buy food-- they don't have the encrypted chips that most credit and debit cards do. Cards with chips are harder to skim. On top of that, EBT cards don't have fraud detection services. You know, like those text messages you get about suspicious credit card transactions. Text 1 if it was you. And if not, they'll cancel the transaction.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: And even with debit cards, you can usually call your bank and tell them that I was stolen from yesterday, and you could get your money back. Renee's EBT card didn't have any of that. All of this has turned SNAP recipients into easy marks, even people like Renee, who never lets her card out of her sight. We try to explain all of this to the officer, who listens to Renee's story.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: So we have footage from the--

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: Bowers!

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The officer calls over another cop, Officer Bowers. His supervisor tells him to get the footage from CVS for us. Bowers hops into his patrol car, and we get back into my car to follow him. Then, as we're driving, we notice Bowers' car has its lights flashing.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: I don't know what these lights mean.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: He's serious about his business.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Yeah. It's crazy. We have a freaking police escort to a CVS. What?

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I'm not playing here.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: If this don't make the news. See, we're not playing? Look, he's in front of us, directing us with his lights on.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: When we get there, Bowers talks to the CVS employee, who shows him to the back room. We wait out front in the store for about 15 or 20 minutes. Then Officer Bowers and the CVS employee re-emerge.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, they're out.

segments.speaker: CVS Employee
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Same one?

segments.speaker: Officer Bowers
segments.text: That's them, yeah.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Bowers told us it was the same woman, the one in a low bun, in a blue-striped skirt, buying hundreds of dollars of baby formula.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: OK. They hit up all the stores, then.

segments.speaker: Officer Bowers
segments.text: OK. Yup. Give me one second.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Are we able to get the video?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Officer Bowers shows us the security footage, which he recorded on his phone. We see the woman getting into the same silver minivan after.

segments.speaker: Officer Bowers
segments.text: We do have a vehicle. It's a Toyota Sienna.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Yeah, mhm.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Yeah, same one from the other.

segments.speaker: Officer Bowers
segments.text: Yeah. So I think this is a West Virginia tag.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The license plate, the thing that could lead them to the criminals-- it's blurry here too. But Bowers says he'd use some fancy police tool to try to figure it out. Finally, the runaround had landed Renee somewhere. She'd found someone in a position of authority actually willing to help her.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: A few days later, Officer Bowers calls me. He won't let me record or conference Renee in, so I have to tell her afterward what he said.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: OK. Hey, Renee.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: I tell her that Bowers said he thinks he found a match for the license plate, but he couldn't hand that information over to her.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: His supervisor will no longer let him work on the case.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Yeah, because Baltimore County already has an investigation and that-- it can only be done through Baltimore County now.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Oh, my god.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: And so Renee's case landed back in the hands of the cop who wasn't answering her texts or calls. Renee understood Bowers was just following his boss's orders, but still.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: It feels like, even though it wasn't his fault, it's like all these other people let me down. So when we went there and they actually helped us, I was so excited. I was so excited. I was thinking, OK, well, he was going to call and we're going to have some news saying that they caught these people or something, just something. And then now he's doing the same, just like every other one did.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I don't know what to think anymore. I mean, I could try to call Officer Valis. But if he's not answering my texts, he's not going to answer the calls either.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: I have no idea.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Now, I can-- I can contact the guy from the OIG. He was really nice, but nobody's saying anything.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: Just kind of keeping me in the dark, like-- you know. I don't know. It's just weird to me. Like, this happened to me. I am not some kind of-- the suspect. I am the victim that this happened to.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: (VOICE BREAKING) I'm just tired of all. I'm tired of all of it.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: I'm so sorry, Renee.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: It's just frustrating, you know? You get in touch with all these people. They promise to keep you updated, promise to call you back, and nothing. It makes you think, like, why did I even ask for their help in the first place? So, I mean, I don't know what else to do. I've done everything I could. There's nothing else for me to do.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: While she was trying to run down this $3,000, there was so much else going on in her life. There always is. In the last couple of months, a cracked tooth from stress, busted brakes on her minivan. She had to give away her dog. They couldn't afford it. One day, her carbon monoxide alarm randomly went off, and she had to call the fire department to sort it out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But surprisingly, the day after I broke the news to her about Bowers, she managed to get in touch with the cop who had been ghosting her for weeks. Remember Officer Valis, the Baltimore County cop who, this whole time, was supposed to be looking into her case? She'd reached him, in a very kind of private detective sort of way.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: So yesterday, I kept calling Officer Valis. His phone is still going right to voicemail. I said, this is weird. Why-- if it's a cell phone from work, why would it be off all the time? And then finally, I said, you know what? Something told me, try from a different phone. So do you know, I called from my son's phone, and it rang.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: [BRENNA GASPS]

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I said, oh, my god. I think he blocked my number.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Oh, my god.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: And I was so furious when I got in touch with him. He's all like, hello? And I'm like, hi, Officer Valis? He's like, who is this? I said, this is Renee. I said, you're the one handling my case.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: I said, I'm wondering if, like, you blocked my number. And it made me sound like a creep, but I was so mad. And I'm like, I have been trying to contact you. And he-- then, once I mentioned about being blocked, he started being super nice to me. And I said that you guys should be getting this information, not me-- not me and the news reporter. We have been getting it. We went to the source to get the footage, nobody else.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: And then he started-- he was, like, you know, try to stay strong. We're trying. And he gave me a number to another-- like Crime Stoppers, or something like that. He said they will get on this more than anybody else. Like, what do you mean, they will get on this?

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: You guys-- if you can't leave your area that you're patrolling, then somebody should be going there and doing this. Then he also tells me that, yeah, I'm pretty sure. I thought you could open another case in another area. I said, well, the other guy told me that his boss said something different, and he don't think-- this is what I mean about the runaround.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: We reached out to the Baltimore county police department. They said Officer Valis did block Renee's member, quote, "for a brief period of time." But they also said he was working on her case. And after Renee got through to Valis, he did start updating her more. He told her police found the skimmer that they think was used to steal her card number.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: But then, in November, Renee lost the appeal she had filed. The judge complimented Renee's tenacity, saying she'd quote, "single-handedly and capably investigated the crime and identified suspects." But the judge also said that there's nothing in Maryland law that requires social services to repay stolen SNAP funds.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: And so Renee wasn't going to get her money back. But she was still looking for some way. And an attorney who volunteered to help her with her case said, there is a way. You can appeal the appeal. Renee thought it over.

segments.speaker: Renee
segments.text: She's like, it's up to you. Do you want to do another appeal? And I'm like, no. I said, what's the purpose? Like, just to be let down over and over by different judges that are saying, I'm sorry. But then on the other hand, it's like, I already came this far. Why not try to have another appeal and do it again? My mind just goes back and forth. Like, should I, shouldn't I? Should I or shouldn't I?

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: Answer-- I should. She filed a second appeal. There is actually one other way this whole thing could be fixed. Congress could do something. And, kind of amazingly, they sort of have.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The huge spending bill Congress passed last month requires states to reimburse people who have had their SNAP benefits stolen. It's not going to help Renee though. It only applies to thefts since October. Hers was in August. Also, it ends in 2024, so it's a temporary fix.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: But Renee's story did get noticed. She actually testified before the state senate. And later, her congressmen, who had been following this issue, introduced a bill that would fix things in a permanent way. It has bipartisan support and looks like it might actually go somewhere.

segments.speaker: Brenna Smith
segments.text: The runaround-- it's a thing that can happen to you, but it can also be a strategy. You just stay in it until someone notices and does something.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Brenna Smith. She's an investigative reporter with the Baltimore Banner, where a version of her story first appeared. The story was produced by Chris Benderev.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, a nine-year-old on a runaround that his dad does not understand. That's in a minute on Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, "The Runaround." Stories of all kinds of runarounds that people find themselves trapped in, test who they are. And other sorts of runarounds as well. We have arrived at Act Two of our program. Act Two, "Strange Loop."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So we now turn to a different kind of runaround. And the person you're going to hear about next, nobody is giving him the runaround. He's just running around, for reasons that are mysterious even to those who are closest to him. David Kestenbaum talked to him about it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The guy doing this running around in circles, he's nine years old. And I know him because I live with him. My son, Max, started doing this early in the pandemic.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Max was one of those kids where virtual school was really impossible. All those faces and little boxes on the screen, he just could not focus or stay with it. His handwriting was crazy. He sometimes struggled to read his own name. At some point, we realized he didn't know the months of the year. He had big hills to climb. I worried.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: One day, he hit on this idea of running loops around the block. We live on a weird lollipop of a street, so these were actual loops he was running, around and around. The neighbors told us he was sometimes the only other person they would see during the day. One time, an older man came out and gave him cookies.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The running around seemed to settle his mind in a way I did not fully understand. Virtual school was tears and frustration, but running these loops reset him somehow. It was more than just getting exercise. I could see him talking to himself as he went by, but I had no idea what he was saying.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He's been doing it for years now, sometimes several times a day. "I'm going for a run around the block. Sound of door closing, and then he'll be gone, sometimes for 20 minutes.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He's done it first thing in the morning, right out of bed, when it's still dark. He does it in the rain-- annoyingly, never with a raincoat. I pile towels by the door. He'll change clothes, but then an hour later, go out again. He did it when it was -22 wind chill.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: I wanted to eavesdrop on one of these runs to hear what he was saying. Something going on out there was helping him. I wanted to understand his brain. So I had this idea of pinning a small microphone on him. He was not into it. "Max, want to wear this microphone when you run around the block?" Max-- "Next time!" Me-- "Max, I only want you to do this if you want to." Max-- "Not now." And so on.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: But I know how to work a reluctant source. I got him after a run one evening. It was dark and raining. He agreed to a brief interview

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I don't know anything about running. Don't ask me any more questions.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's not an interrogation.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah, it is. I'm tied to a metal chair.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Uh, you're just holding your hands behind your back as if you're tied to a metal chair.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: It counts.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Do you remember the joke you told me the other day about ADHD? What does ADHD stand for?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Attention deficit-- hey, donuts!

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Do you ever feel like that in your head?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah. Like, distracted while doing something.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: And when you're running, does that ever happen?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: No. I'm focused on my running and my story, that's it.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: A story. That's what's going on in his head out there, going around and around. He's telling himself a story. That's what the running unleashed.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I can remember the first story I ever had. It's pretty much just a little chicken, a little duck, and they were literally friends. And they waddled around.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The stories have changed as he's gotten older.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Did you have a story in your head just now?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah. There was this big, red monster. Like, imagine a human, then imagine him completely ash. Like, just ash.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It was interesting to hear this. It has an attention to detail that is sometimes not present in other parts of his life.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Then imagine a little red tinge coming off him. He's like a fire person. His hair's on fire. His eyes are red, like fire.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: He told me another one that was like pieces of the world had lodged in his head and recombined. This one violated multiple copyrights. The Avengers were in it, but then also Spaceman Spiff from "Calvin and Hobbes." And also, somehow--

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I was pretending to be Arthur Dent, I think. Yeah, Arthur Dent.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: From The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What do you think it is about running and a story that is calming?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I don't know. I have no idea.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Are you thinking about a story, like, all day long, kind of?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: All day. I run and wander during recess. And the thing-- and I usually-- sometimes I play with my friends, and sometimes I wander around, thinking about it. But yeah.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Wow, it's like all day long.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yup.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: That's kind of amazing. I didn't know that.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Hm.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Could you think of the story if you were just staying in the house?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah, I could, but it's harder. I could think of one, but it's harder.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Why do you think it's easier when you're running around the block?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Uh, I don't know. Because-- maybe because I'm moving. I don't know why. That's been a strange thing where, if I'm moving, it's completely fine. I have to move to see it. But if I'm standing still, it's really hard.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: It's funny that you're just running in circles, you know?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Like, you're not going anywhere.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Well, in my head, I am. In my head, I am. I outsmarted you. [GIGGLING]

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: What did you say?

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I outsmarted you, Daddy.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: The philosopher, Thomas Nagel, once wrote an essay titled, "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" Apparently, he had bats in his house, and he wondered if it was possible to truly know what it was like to be a bat, to have webbing on your arms, to perceive the world with sonar, to hang upside down in the attic. His answer was, no, you could not know the mind of such a creature.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: OK, should we go?

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Yeah, go.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: OK, bye.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: Max did finally agree to let me put a mic on him while he ran around the block. It was like I was right there with him. He was battling some invisible monster.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: [MAX RUNNING]

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: I'll be fine.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: "I'll be fine." "I'll be fine," he says.

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: Those cuts are deep.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: "Those cuts are deep."

segments.speaker: Max
segments.text: It's fine.

segments.speaker: David Kestenbaum
segments.text: "It's fine." You're right, Max. It is.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: David Kestenbaum is our show's senior editor.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Three, "Americans Most Wanted." So we now turn to criminals trying to give the runaround to the police. And in this case, choosing a route that you see now and then in the movies, they escape to Mexico. That's right, across the border to start a new life in a country where they think that they're going to be safe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So many people do this. In fact, the numbers are on the rise. The Mexican police formed a special elite unit whose only mandate is to catch these fugitives. The unit's based in Baja California, just south of San Diego. They work with tips they get from the FBI and US Marshals. They are called the Gringo Hunters.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Kevin Sieff is a reporter for the Washington Post. He hung out with them as they ran around trying to snag fugitives.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: The cops in this special unit find the gringos everywhere-- in beach resorts, at a nightclub, called Papas & Beer, in cars with sex workers, in Carl's Jr parking lots. Some had undergone plastic surgery and acquired new names they couldn't pronounce. Some were found dead.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: They were former Playboy models, amateur surfers, ex-Navy officers. Most of them are alleged serious criminals-- rapists, pedophiles, murderers. The cops have become used to the way American fugitives saunter across the border, expecting that they won't be found.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Here's Moises. He was the head of the unit when I was there. He's proud of his work, but he gets that it can be kind of funny sometimes.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: There's many Americans, I think, that, like in the cartoons and in the movies, that Mexico-- oh, yeah, everybody there has boots and hat and is on a horse or on a donkey. And so then they think, I can go and hide there. And I mean, they-- when they come here to Mexico and they see, no, this is-- here's a city. I mean, it's a big city. And it's even better. I'll hide, and the police will never find me. And when they least expect it, boom, there we are, right in front of them.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Moises has been doing the job for 12 years. Hanging out with him, he's like an encyclopedia of gringo fugitives. A lot of the gringos, he tells me, are white guys who think they can make a go of hiding on the coast, blending in with tourists, but they can't.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: The way they dress, the way they walk, the way they express themselves is totally different. The t-shirts are different. If they're wearing shorts, the shorts are different, totally different.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Even the shoes are totally different. One officer told me the Americans wear flip-flops that are one size too big, usually with socks. Then there are the Mexican-American fugitives who are still such obvious gringos to Moises and the other cops. They're born in the US. They have family in Mexico, but they can never totally blend in either. Something about them is eventually going to betray them as American.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: That's the kind of fugitive they were chasing when I was with them, a Mexican-American guy named Damion Salinas. He's 20 years old from Fresno, California.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Back in 2020, Salinas had allegedly murdered another man at the scene of a traffic accident. The killing was shocking, seemingly unprovoked, a gunshot at point-blank range. The victim was a 36-year-old mechanic named Joshua Thao. He was like a father to his nieces and nephews, his sister said. Right before he was shot, witnesses said, he shook the murderer's hand, trying to calm tempers.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: After the shooting, Salinas vanished. There were no leads. He'd been a fugitive for almost two years. Now, suddenly, there was new intel. Salinas was supposedly here in Ensenada, about an hour and a half south of the border, cutting hair at a barbershop.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Abigail, one of the unit's officers, was leading the planning. They didn't have a search warrant, so they were going to have to find a way to lure Salinas outside.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I don't know. Maybe if their car is outside, we can be, like-- maybe, like, find a way to be like, oh, you got a flat tire or something. Could you come out? I think your car has a flat tire. And then when they go out, that's when we get them. We've done that before.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Abigail is the only woman on the team. You'd think she's the boss, even though she's not. She's on her phone constantly, pumping her sources and colleagues for more and better intel. That's what she was doing during the Salinas case, shouting a stream of questions into her phone.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Did Salinas have any connection to Mexico? Who was he living with? Where was he getting his money from? She paused at one point to catch her breath. "Sorry," she said to her colleague. "It's a murder case, so it's a little bit urgent."

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: We get to the barbershop. Abigail and her colleague, Ivan, scope it out from the front seat. Ivan is a former bodyguard. He's the one on the team most likely to show up with a six pack after a big win. He gets a text. There's intel from the US Marshals.

segments.speaker: Ivan
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Ivan
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: It was a new tip. They're sending us to another barbershop, Ivan says.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Ivan
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: It sounds like Salinas is in Tijuana, about an hour north. So Abigail floors it along the highway that traces the Pacific Ocean, driving close to 100 miles an hour.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Signs of the gringo presence are everywhere, big billboards in English that say things like "Invest In Your New Ocean View House." Another said "Thong and Tequila Party." In some ways, this part of Mexico seems perfect for Americans trying to disappear. But Abigail has become a pro at drawing them out.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: She told me earlier that morning about one of her new strategies. She's created a bunch of fake Facebook accounts using stock photos of attractive women that she uses to catfish fugitives. One guy had actually posted on a Facebook group looking to meet people. He even used his real name.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: He wanted to smoke some weed, and he wanted to smoke it with me, and stay overnight at my place, and have a crazy night. And I said, yes.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: So yeah, he brought his little suitcase with his clothes, and he thought he was going to stay with me for a few days, all, like, washed up and cologned.

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Another cop from the unit cuts in and starts to troll Abigail. "Sometimes they arrive stinky," he says. "It's so you don't have to struggle with the stinky perp, right?" he says. "You just want to deliver them nice and clean, no fuss, back to the gringos."

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Abigail grew up in Tijuana, secretly dreaming of becoming a police officer. Her mother begged her not to. Being a cop was dangerous. But she says she was born to do the job. Abigail waited until her own daughter was a little over two, and then she signed up.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: The stakes feel so high to her. The gringos coming across, they could just repeat their crimes on her side of the border. She told me about the case of a pedophile who fled the US. He moved into a house near a Tijuana elementary school where he was getting ready to look for more kids to abuse. She was like, if we don't catch this guy today, who knows what he'll do here in Mexico?

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: When we arrived in Tijuana, we parked across from the second barbershop and Ivan and Abigail began their surveillance. As always, they work undercover. Today, jeans and t-shirts, like two friends headed out for a day at the beach.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Abigail bought some nachos from the shop next door, slyly peering into the barber shop. Ivan put on a black backpack and walked by-- disguised, I guess, as a 30-something-year-old student. Then we all settled in the car and got comfortable staring through the windshield.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Usually on stakeouts, Ivan is constantly turning up the volume on Bad Bunny. Today, he's kind of bragging, showing me dozens of photos of the gringos he's arrested, like a yearbook of American fugitives. Then they get another call.

segments.speaker: Officer
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Someone has left the apartment above the barbershop. The person got into a gold Honda Accord and drove away. One of the agents says over the radio, "I think it's Salinas." Then they take off, cutting across four lanes of traffic. Abigail cuts off the Honda and they surround the car.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: I'm watching them approach the car and this is kind of a scary moment. Only a few weeks before, the cops had been in a shootout with a fugitive from California. Moises and Ivan got shot. The team told me that they were worried that Salinas too might come out shooting if he was cornered.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: I watch them pull a skinny guy out of the driver's seat and push him against the car. He didn't look to me like the guy I'd seen in the Most Wanted posters. Then they take his wallet from his back pocket. There's a California driver's license with the name Damion Salinas. They get out their handcuffs.

segments.speaker: Officer 1
segments.text: What's your name?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Damion.

segments.speaker: Officer 1
segments.text: Damion, OK. Do you have other ID? Only have this?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Only that, so. It's valid.

segments.speaker: Officer 1
segments.text: You have something you might-- in the car?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Officer 1
segments.text: Nothing. Gun?

segments.speaker: Officer 2
segments.text: You have guns?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Officer 2
segments.text: Drugs?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: No. [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Officer 1
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Even after all the build up, there was still something startling about seeing the cops catch their fugitive. It was surreal. They start figuring out logistics. Who's going to take the gold Honda? Salinas seems confused. He starts saying, "I will go--" And that's when Abigail interrupts him. "No, you're coming with us."

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Abigail
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Salinas doesn't put up a fight. They stick him in the backseat of the car, and I ask if I can sit next to him to ask a few questions. They say sure, but they put the biggest cop in the unit between us, in case Salinas lunges at me. But he doesn't. He looks like he'd just woken up from a nap.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Yeah, I'm not a-- just to be clear, I'm not a law enforcement official. I'm-- I'm a journalist.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Wait, you're--

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Sorry?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: What are you again?

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: I'm a journalist.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Journalist?

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Those are badass jobs. I like them.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: It's interesting, sometimes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This whole day, I'd been wondering, what is this guy going to be like? How had he evaded authorities for almost two years? I think I'd been expecting an angry, sophisticated criminal. This guy, after all, was being accused of homicide.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But Salinas is like a kid trying to disguise himself as a man. His mustache is wispy. He's wearing Air Jordan sandals with socks. "Forever West Coast" was tattooed on his right arm.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: I'm a good dude, man.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: He keeps saying how nervous he is, but then he spins a tale about how he'd only been caught because he let his guard down.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Why didn't you try to go further into Mexico? Like, you stayed so close to the border.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Well, I mean, I'm not a dumbass though. I know why they caught me. I just stopped trying after a while, you know? Things got-- you know? The cops are not really that smart, you know? So every place they hit, I was right-- I was always watching them. I watched them like they watched me. And after a while, I just gave up. I was like, fuck it.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Why'd you give up?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: I was just going through a lot, you know, being alone and shit, the depression.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: You know, PTSD kicks in, all kinds of shit, so.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: So you basically were like-- resigned yourself to getting caught. Almost wanted to get caught, it sounds like.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Yeah, basically. Sometimes, I get--

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Abigail weaves through Tijuana traffic with the siren on. We're headed to the border to hand Salinas over to US authorities. And then Ivan puts on "Gangsta's Paradise" and turns up the volume. He tells me, "Ask him if he's a rapper."

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Are you a rapper? Or were you ever a rapper?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Yeah, I like rap.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Ivan
segments.text: You have a song?

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Have you ever sung a song?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Nah, no. I never.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: And then they pull up a video on Ivan's cell phone. It's a video of Salinas rapping, taken from his social media.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: [SALINAS RAPPING]

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: Oh, yeah. That's me.

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Why-- why did you lie and say you didn't have a song if you had a song?

segments.speaker: Damion Salinas
segments.text: I'm not getting embarrassed, man. That's why.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Salinas seems calm at this point. Abigail parks the car at the border and the Mexican police march Salinas past a long line of people, the daily border crossers and migrants who are waiting to enter the US on foot. They crane their necks to look at the American fugitive. A small group of uniformed US officials is standing at the border. One of the agents bends his knees in a blocker's position, as if Salinas might make a run for it.

segments.speaker: Border Agent
segments.text: Yeah, we know. We know all about it, so. We got-- we got the phone calls. You guys want to bring him? Come on in. All right, thanks, man. He's coming with us.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: The Mexican police take off the Mexican handcuffs and the Americans put on American cuffs. It feels almost ceremonial. The arrest is done, the gringo is back in gringo hands.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: I watched the Gringo Hunters walk back from the border to their car. They had just arrested an alleged murderer. I look for some kind of reaction. I'm not sure what, exactly-- a high five, a look of accomplishment, but there was almost nothing. The unit chases and catches so many gringos that Salinas was just another name on their list. They already had their next day's assignment-- a woman had kidnapped and drugged a child. They too were likely living in Tijuana.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: A few weeks after the Salinas chase, I was talking to Moises, the head of the Gringo Hunters, and he told me this thing. He said that sometimes he's hanging out with his friends who are not cops, and he gets this feeling that I think cops everywhere get, that regular people just don't know how many bad guys are out there. They don't know how scary it can feel to chase fugitive Americans day in and day out.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: What I do is so that, right now, you guys can all be hanging out here comfortably. Because if we didn't do it, we'd be surrounded by all these kind of people. Like, we wouldn't be able to just hang out in the afternoons and the evenings, because we'd just be looking over our shoulder.

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Because we've caught an infinite number of Americans, eh? I've participated in, I don't know, around 1,300, 1,200 fugitive arrests. I mean, that's a lot of fugitives we've arrested. That's two or three per week, 140, 150 a year, per year.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: And it never ends, right? They just keep on coming.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, they just keep on coming. They keep on coming. And I mean, there are times when things slow down, but then suddenly it's like-- like they all agree to come across at the same time. I don't know. I like to say that they all came on the same bus or something.

segments.speaker: Moises
segments.text: [SPEAKING SPANISH]

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: Moises doesn't come out and say it, but chasing American fugitives all day, it has shaped how he sees the United States. Part of the problem, he says, is that in the US, it's so easy to get a gun. On some of his trips there, it seemed like everyone was armed.

segments.speaker: Kevin Sieff
segments.text: As we talked, it struck me that he'd come to see Mexico as being in a perilous position, bordering this heavily-armed, crime-infested nation. I had heard that tone before. He spoke with a very real fear and perhaps a little bit of hysteria, the same way I've heard so many Americans talk about a lawless Mexico.
